name: Joab
charge: Murder of Abner and Amasa in time of peace
summary: David's general killed Abner in the gate of Hebron under cover of a private word, avenging Asahel's death in battle, and years later killed Amasa with a kiss and a hidden sword. David laid both on Solomon's charge.
offense: Abner killed Asahel in battle after repeatedly warning him to turn aside. Later Abner came to David to bring Israel under his rule, and the king sent him away in peace (2 Samuel 2:19-23; 3:12-21). Joab recalled him without David's knowledge, took him aside as if to speak privately, and killed him for Asahel's blood (2 Samuel 3:26-30). He turned a peaceful meeting into revenge. David declared himself and his kingdom guiltless of Abner's blood, mourned openly, and said the Lord would reward the evildoer according to his wickedness (2 Samuel 3:28-39). Joab's military importance did not change what he had done. The man who served the throne had acted against the peace the king had given. He later killed Amasa, the captain appointed in his place. He greeted him as a brother, took him by the beard as if to kiss him, and struck him with the sword (2 Samuel 19:13; 20:8-10). The greeting concealed the blow. David's final charge gathered Abner and Amasa together: Joab had shed the blood of war in peace (1 Kings 2:5-6). Experience in battle did not authorize treachery outside it.
judgment: When Solomon acted against Adonijah's party, Joab fled to the tabernacle and caught the horns of the altar. Benaiah summoned him, but he refused to come out and said he would die there (1 Kings 2:28-30). The place of worship could not be made a defence against responsibility for deliberate murder.

entries.commentary: There was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David, but David waxed stronger and stronger and the house of Saul weaker and weaker. Each had those that followed him, but the Most High increased David because he had been anointed to be the next king over Israel.

Sons were born to David in Hebron: the firstborn Amnon of Ahinoam, Chileab of Abigail, Absalom the son of Maachah the daughter of the king of Geshur, Adonijah the son of Haggith, Shephatiah of Abital, and Ithream of Eglah his wife. Abner made himself strong for the house of Saul. When Ishbosheth charged him over Rizpah, Saul's concubine, Abner was very wroth, saying he had shown kindness to the house of Saul and not delivered them to David, and now was charged with a fault concerning this woman. Abner swore to do to himself and more, to translate the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and Judah, from Dan even to Beersheba. Ishbosheth could not answer him a word, because he feared him. Abner was through with Ishbosheth and turned to go with David and the Lord.

Abner sent messengers to David offering to bring all Israel to him. David agreed to make a league, but required that Michal, Saul's daughter, first be brought to him, and he sent to Ishbosheth to deliver his wife whom he had espoused for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines. Michal was taken from her husband Phaltiel, who went weeping behind her until Abner told him to return. David was taking back what was his as the king before the Lord. Abner spoke with the elders of Israel and with Benjamin, reminding them they had sought David in times past, and that the Lord had said by the hand of David He would save Israel out of the hand of the Philistines and all their enemies. Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, David made them a feast, and Abner went in peace to gather all Israel to David.

Joab returned from pursuing a troop and heard that Abner had come and been sent away in peace. Joab came to the king and said Abner had come to deceive him and to know his going out and coming in; he did not trust Abner, and there was already blood between them, for Abner had killed Asahel his brother. Joab, without David's knowledge, sent messengers after Abner and brought him back to Hebron, took him aside in the gate to speak quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother. It was payback; Joab's blood was burning for revenge. Abner was unwise to return to that place, knowing what Joab would do, but it was of the Lord.

When David heard it, he declared himself and his kingdom guiltless before the Lord forever from the blood of Abner, and laid it on the head of Joab and all his father's house. He commanded Joab and all the people to rend their clothes and gird with sackcloth and mourn before Abner, and the king himself followed the coffin. David wept at the grave and lamented over Abner in the spirit, another eulogy and prophecy: Abner died as a fool dieth, his hands not bound nor his feet in fetters, but he fell as a man falleth before wicked men. All the people wept again and took notice, and David swore not to taste bread till the sun went down, and it pleased the people; whatsoever the king did pleased them, for David was in the right spirit and the Lord was dealing with the nation. David said he was weak that day though anointed king, and that the sons of Zeruiah were too hard for him, ruthless men he could not bring under; but the Lord would reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness. That payback came later through Solomon concerning Joab.

A man of Belial, a devil, named Sheba the son of Bichri, blew a trumpet and cried that they had no part in David nor inheritance in the son of Jesse, and every man of Israel went up from David to follow Sheba, while the men of Judah clave unto the king from Jordan to Jerusalem. David came to his house in Jerusalem and took the ten concubines Absalom had defiled, put them in ward, and fed them but went not in unto them; they were shut up in widowhood until the day of their death because Absalom had gone in unto them.

David told Amasa to assemble the men of Judah within three days, but Amasa tarried longer than the set time. So David sent Abishai with Joab's men, the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men to pursue Sheba lest he escape into fenced cities. At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab came to Amasa with a sword secretly fastened, took him by the beard with his right hand as if to kiss him, and smote him in the fifth rib so that his bowels shed to the ground, and he died at one stroke. Joab was grimy and shady, murdering the man who had been named captain in his place. One of Joab's men stood by Amasa calling all who favored Joab and David to follow after Joab. Amasa wallowed in his blood in the midst of the highway, and when the people stood still to look, the man removed him into the field and cast a cloth over him, and then all the people went on after Joab to pursue Sheba.

Joab pursued Sheba through all the tribes to Abel of Beth-maachah, and they cast up a bank against the city and battered the wall to throw it down. A wise woman of the city called out to Joab, reminding him of the old saying that men would surely ask counsel at Abel, and asked why he would swallow up a city that was a mother in Israel and the inheritance of the Lord. Joab answered that he did not seek to destroy, but only wanted Sheba the son of Bichri, who had lifted up his hand against the king; deliver him and he would depart. The woman promised that Sheba's head would be thrown over the wall. She went to all the people in her wisdom, and they cut off Sheba's head and cast it out to Joab, who blew the trumpet and retired from the city, every man to his tent, and returned to Jerusalem unto the king.

Joab was over all the host of Israel, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada over the Cherethites and the Pelethites. Adoram was over the tribute, Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder, and Sheva was scribe. Zadok and Abiathar were the priests, and Ira the Jairite was a chief ruler about David. Do not read merely to say you read four chapters; read and truly study to give the sense and understand the scriptures. --- Topics: [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

The days of David draw near that he should die, and he charges Solomon to be strong, to keep the charge of the Lord his God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes, commandments, and judgments as written in the law of Moses, that he may prosper. There was a stipulation for the throne to continue: if his children take heed to their way and walk before the Most High in truth with all their heart, the throne stands. Reading through the kings, we see many who broke the commandments, and among their children some were righteous and some unrighteous. -
Solomon thrusts out Abiathar from being priest unto the Lord, fulfilling the word the Most High spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh. The old judgment on Eli's line is carried out.

Joab, who had turned after Adonijah, flees to the tabernacle of the Lord and catches hold of the horns of the altar, but Solomon sends Benaiah to fall upon him. Joab dies for the innocent blood he shed when he slew Abner and Amasa, two men more righteous and better than he, without David's knowledge. The blood returns upon Joab's own head and upon his seed, while upon David and his seed and throne there shall be peace forever from the Lord. Benaiah is set over the host in his place.

Shimei is commanded to build a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, never crossing the brook Kidron on pain of death, and he agrees. After three years he goes to Gath after his runaway servants and breaks the oath, so Solomon has Benaiah put him to death, and the kingdom is established in Solomon's hand.

If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve, and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing. If he came in by himself he goes out by himself; if he were married when he came in, his wife goes out with him. Deuteronomy repeats the same judgment for a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman sold unto thee. [Nehemiah 5](/bible/nehemiah/5) shows how brethren came into servitude: in the dearth some mortgaged lands, vineyards, and houses to buy corn, some borrowed money for the king's tribute, and some brought their sons and daughters into bondage. The brother that waxes poor is not to be compelled to serve as a bondservant, but as an hired servant, and not ruled over harshly. If the master gave him a wife and she bare him sons or daughters, the wife and her children are the master's, and he goes out by himself; he did not bring them in. His two choices are to go out alone, or to plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children, have his ear bored through with an aul at the door post, and serve his master for ever. Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

If a man sell his daughter to be a maidservant, she shall not go out as the menservants do. The reason is that her master betrothed her to himself, or unto his son; she is a wife, not a six-year servant, so the release of the menservants does not apply to her. If she please not her master who hath betrothed her to himself, he must let her be redeemed; he has no power to sell her unto a strange nation, seeing he hath dealt deceitfully with her. The deceit is that he betrothed her to himself and then would not deal with her, keeping her to himself when she could have been another man's wife. If he take him another wife, her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage shall he not diminish; the duty of marriage is the marriage bed. If he lay with her, she belongs to him and he cannot send her away; and if he do not these three unto her, then shall she go out free without money. He must take care of her.

If a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand, a place was appointed whither he shall flee. That is the case of the slayer that kills his neighbour ignorantly, as when a man hews wood with his neighbour and the axe head slips from the helve and lights upon him that he die: he flees to the appointed city and lives, lest the avenger of blood overtake him while his heart is hot, for he was not worthy of death, having hated him not in time past. But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour to slay him with guile, thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die. Men would run and grab the horns of the altar, but wilful murder found no refuge there.

If men strive and one smite another so that he keep his bed, he that smote him shall pay for the loss of his time and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed. That is restitution: paying for the time the man was down and could not work and provide for his family. That is what the court system calls a civil suit today.

If a man smite his servant with a rod and he die under his hand, he shall surely be punished; but if he continue a day or two, he shall not be punished, for he is his money. The wisdom writings teach not to be ashamed of much correction of children, nor of making the side of an evil servant to bleed. An evil servant that will not get right could be corrected physically, so long as he was not killed.

If men strive and hurt a woman with child so that her fruit depart from her, this judgment covers the miscarriage: if no mischief follow, he is punished as the woman's husband lays upon him and the judges determine; and if any mischief follow, then life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, wound for wound.

If an ox gore a man or a woman that they die, the ox is stoned and his flesh not eaten, and the owner is quit. But if the ox were wont to push with his horns in time past, and it hath been testified to his owner, and he hath not kept him in, and it kill a man or a woman, the ox is stoned and his owner also put to death. Most do not have oxen today, but the same judgment reaches the yard dogs, the pit bulls, German shepherds, and rottweilers. If the dog has bitten before and it was reported to you, and it gets out again through a snapped chain or a breach in the fence and mauls or kills somebody, the scripture holds the owner responsible unto death; that is why animal control writes the ticket and warns you to keep your dogs in. The law is slack right now, as Habakkuk says, so many punishments worthy of death in the scriptures, like rape or this judgment, come out today as a fine or a slap on the hand.

When the Most High cut off the nations of the land of Canaan, the Canaanites, the Jebusites, the Perizzites, and the Girgashites, and Israel succeeded them and dwelt in their cities and houses, Israel was to separate three cities in the midst of the land and prepare the way to them. This law goes into accidental death, what the Bible sometimes calls manslaughter. An Israelite who accidentally killed another could flee to one of these three cities of refuge, where the avenger of blood could not seek him out and kill him there to revenge the blood of his nearest of kin.

Whoso killeth his neighbour ignorantly, whom he hated not in time past, means he did not mean to do it; it was an accident. The example given is two men hewing wood, and the axe head slips from the helve and strikes the neighbour that he die: he shall flee to one of those cities and live. The avenger of blood is the nearest of kin, and while his heart is hot he may pursue and overtake the slayer because the way is long. But the slayer was not worthy of death, because he hated him not in time past; there was no premeditation, no intention to kill. Accidents happen, and the Most High put laws in place for when these things happened. If it was for sure an accident, the man is not worthy of death, as the scripture says.

If the Lord enlarge thy coast as he sware unto the fathers, then three more cities were to be added. As Israel grew and possessed more of the land of Canaan, more cities of refuge were established where a slayer could flee from the avenger of blood. The purpose is stated plainly: that innocent blood be not shed in the land which the Lord giveth thee for an inheritance, and so blood be upon thee.

This gives the distinction between an accident and intentional killing; this is describing murder. He hated his neighbour and lay in wait for him: he devised a scheme, waited for the right opportunity and the right time, rose up against him, and smote him mortally that he died. The murderer cannot then run to a city of refuge to lay low. Those cities were not established for him; they were established so retaliation did not come on those who accidentally brought harm to somebody. The elders of his own city shall fetch him from there and deliver him into the hand of the avenger of blood, that he may die. Thine eye shall not pity him: putting away the guilt of innocent blood from Israel is what makes it go well with the nation.

What is a landmark? It pays to use tools outside the scriptures, because what good is reading the Bible without understanding of the words written in it. The Zondervan Bible Dictionary defines a landmark as an object, stone, or post used to mark the boundary of a field, and notes that removal of landmarks was prohibited by the Mosaic law. The landmark establishes the boundaries of a man's property, where it begins and where it ends. A man who keeps nudging his neighbour's landmark over little by little until he has taken an acre is stealing land; the dictionary notes it was considered equal to theft.

One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity or any sin. One man alone saying he saw a theft is not proof; anybody can come and lie and get people put to death, imprisoned, or beaten. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established. It has to be clear-cut; two or three solid witnesses, not one solid witness and a shaky witness. We deal with facts.

When a false witness rises up, both men in the controversy stand before the Lord, before the priests and the judges of those days. False accusation is real: people will lie on a man to cover themselves, and false witnesses arise among your own people as well, which is part of why the nation fell into captivity. The judges shall make diligent inquisition: they get to the bottom of the matter and find out exactly who is telling the truth, who is lying, and what the facts are. A judge cannot judge a matter off what one person says; each side tells the story in his own favour, so you must examine the whole matter, question both sides against each other, and decipher the truth. Diligent inquisition is what separates a good judge from a bad judge; a lazy or partial judge makes false judgment. If the witness is found false, then shall ye do unto him as he had thought to have done unto his brother. Accuse a man falsely of stealing, and the judgment for stealing comes on you; accuse him falsely of adultery or another sin punishable by death, and you are put to death, because that is what you intended for your neighbour. So is evil put away from Israel.
The judgment is public and it teaches: those which remain shall hear and fear, and shall henceforth commit no more any such evil among you.

Thine eye shall not pity: in this time under Moses it was life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot. If a man knocked out your tooth, the recompense was exact, and it went through the judges one way or another; thus saith the law. Christ spoke on this saying, because exact retaliation between men creates a never-ending cycle of vengeance and hatred. Turning the other cheek does not mean letting somebody beat you down into the dirt; it means when somebody does something to you, do not come back later seeking revenge. Seeking revenge only brings more judgment on your own head; the wise course is to let it go and let the Most High repay, for vengeance belongs to him.

verses.text: And when Joab was come out from David, he sent messengers after Abner, which brought him again from the well of Sirah: but David knew it not.
And when Abner was returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside in the gate to speak with him quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.
And afterward when David heard it, he said, I and my kingdom are guiltless before the Lord for ever from the blood of Abner the son of Ner:

Let it rest on the head of Joab, and on all his father’s house; and let there not fail from the house of Joab one that hath an issue, or that is a leper, or that leaneth on a staff, or that falleth on the sword, or that lacketh bread.
So Joab and Abishai his brother slew Abner, because he had slain their brother Asahel at Gibeon in the battle.
And the king said unto his servants, Know ye not that there is a prince and a great man fallen this day in Israel?
And I am this day weak, though anointed king; and these men the sons of Zeruiah be too hard for me: the Lord shall reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness.

When they were at the great stone which is in Gibeon, Amasa went before them. And Joab’s garment that he had put on was girded unto him, and upon it a girdle with a sword fastened upon his loins in the sheath thereof; and as he went forth it fell out.
And Joab said to Amasa, Art thou in health, my brother? And Joab took Amasa by the beard with the right hand to kiss him.

But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab’s hand: so he smote him therewith in the fifth rib, and shed out his bowels to the ground, and struck him not again; and he died. So Joab and Abishai his brother pursued after Sheba the son of Bichri.

Moreover thou knowest also what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, and what he did to the two captains of the hosts of Israel, unto Abner the son of Ner, and unto Amasa the son of Jether, whom he slew, and shed the blood of war in peace, and put the blood of war upon his girdle that was about his loins, and in his shoes that were on his feet.
Do therefore according to thy wisdom, and let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace.
Then tidings came to Joab: for Joab had turned after Adonijah, though he turned not after Absalom. And Joab fled unto the tabernacle of the Lord, and caught hold on the horns of the altar.
And it was told king Solomon that Joab was fled unto the tabernacle of the Lord; and, behold, he is by the altar. Then Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, Go, fall upon him.

And Benaiah came to the tabernacle of the Lord, and said unto him, Thus saith the king, Come forth. And he said, Nay; but I will die here. And Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me.
And the king said unto him, Do as he hath said, and fall upon him, and bury him; that thou mayest take away the innocent blood, which Joab shed, from me, and from the house of my father.

And the Lord shall return his blood upon his own head, who fell upon two men more righteous and better than he, and slew them with the sword, my father David not knowing thereof, to wit, Abner the son of Ner, captain of the host of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, captain of the host of Judah.

Their blood shall therefore return upon the head of Joab, and upon the head of his seed for ever: but upon David, and upon his seed, and upon his house, and upon his throne, shall there be peace for ever from the Lord.
So Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up, and fell upon him, and slew him: and he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.
But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour, to slay him with guile; thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die.
But if any man hate his neighbour, and lie in wait for him, and rise up against him, and smite him mortally that he die, and fleeth into one of these cities:
Then the elders of his city shall send and fetch him thence, and deliver him into the hand of the avenger of blood, that he may die.
Thine eye shall not pity him, but thou shalt put away the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, that it may go well with thee.

lawsResolved.text: If a man acts with premeditation against his neighbor, to kill him with guile, he shall die.
One who strikes a man so that he dies is a murderer and shall be put to death.
If a murder flees to a city of refuge, he is to be turned over to the hand of the executioner that he may die.
God requires the blood of a murderer for it defiles the land.
You are not to personally avenge or bear any grudge against your brethren.

But if any man hate his neighbour, and lie in wait for him, and rise up against him, and smite him mortally that he die, and fleeth into one of these cities:
Then the elders of his city shall send and fetch him thence, and deliver him into the hand of the avenger of blood, that he may die.
Thine eye shall not pity him, but thou shalt put away the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, that it may go well with thee.
